scoreScale.endpointReachability: A bound only; physical combinations and profile mappings need not attain both endpoints.

purposes.method: 100 × sum(value × declared integer weight) / sum(all declared weights), only when every contribution is observed. Classification maps favorable:+1, neutral:0, caution:−1. Phase preference and Mercury-hour matching are explicitly separate editorial mappings.
purposes.tiePolicy: Same numerator and denominator within a profile/case form a tie; dates may provide stable display order only.
limitations: Phase preference assigns +1 to waxing and −1 to waning only for this declared comparison. Lunar speed thresholds and applying-aspect approximation retain their inherited qualifications.
Scores are modern editorial study indices, not historical formulae, probabilities, religious efficacy, personal advice or objectively good/bad days.
Only the explicit sampled instant is described. A local-noon sample does not classify the whole date; different observer-local noons are different instants.
Compare scores only within the same declared profile and case. A shared numerical scale does not make different traditions or observers commensurable.
Dependency groups expose repeated measurements and each declared group budget; they are accounting groups, not independent evidence. Several groups still reuse the same Moon and Sun positions.
All required contributions must be observed. Missing, unavailable or unresolved rules make score null; absent data is never favorable and is never removed from the denominator.
Equal exact score numerators under the same denominator are ties. Stable display order within a tie is not a stronger result.
No observed religious festival, calendar label, eclipse, eschatology, birth chart, oracle draw or source-only reference contributes to these profiles.

traditions.label: Christian traditions · selected texts and teachings
traditions.scope: Mark plus current Catholic and Seventh-day Adventist statements; not all Christian denominations.
traditions.summary: The selected sources discuss Christ’s return, judgment and watchfulness while withholding a known day or hour.

eschatology.summary: Mark 13:32–37 withholds the time. Catholic Catechism 673 and current Adventist teaching likewise give no revealed date; their wider doctrinal accounts remain distinct.
eschatology.dateability: No independently validated modern calendar date is supplied by this selected reference.

calendarNotes: Separately sourced Christian feast dates and computus variants belong to the observance layer; they do not date the Second Coming.
limitations: No single Catholic or Adventist statement represents every Christian community.
Historical date-setting movements are not silently substituted for these current statements.

traditions.label: Jewish traditions · selected rabbinic messianism
traditions.scope: Selected Sanhedrin passages and Maimonides; not an exhaustive account of Jewish belief.
traditions.summary: The checked rabbinic passages preserve debate about redemption and explicitly warn against calculating its end date.

eschatology.summary: Sanhedrin 97b records conflicting historical calculations and criticism of failed deadlines. Maimonides, Kings and Wars 12:1–2, distinguishes messianic hope from a certain sequence or date and describes the ordinary natural order continuing.
eschatology.dateability: No independently validated modern calendar date is supplied by this selected reference.

calendarNotes: A Hebrew civil date or a sourced festival rule is not a messianic countdown. Observance location, boundary and community variants remain in the dated layer.
limitations: Multiple Talmudic speakers are not one unanimous prediction.
Maimonides is one influential formulation; later Jewish traditions are not exhaustively covered.

traditions.label: Islamic traditions · the Hour in selected Qur’anic verses
traditions.scope: Qur’an 7:187 and 31:34 in one named English translation; detailed Sunni/Shia traditions not surveyed.
traditions.summary: The selected verses place knowledge of the Hour with God rather than supplying people with a calendar deadline.

eschatology.summary: Qur’an 7:187 and 31:34 explicitly reserve knowledge of the Hour to God. This reference therefore provides no dated end-time event.
eschatology.dateability: No independently validated modern calendar date is supplied by this selected reference.

calendarNotes: Calculated Islamic civil/Umm al-Qura labels and observed lunar starts are different methods. Neither calendar conversion dates the Hour.
limitations: Two verses from one text/translation are not independent predictive confirmations.
Mahdi, resurrection and end-time sign traditions require their own named sources; they are not synthesized here.

traditions.label: Hindu traditions · selected Vaiṣṇava renewal narratives
traditions.scope: Bhāgavata 12.2 and Bhagavad Gītā 4.7–8 in named modern Vaiṣṇava translations.
traditions.summary: These passages describe restoration of dharma and, in the Bhāgavata, Kalki followed by a renewed age.

eschatology.summary: Bhāgavata 12.2.18–23 describes Kalki and Satya-yuga. Verse 24 gives a Sun–Moon–Bṛhaspati/Puṣya condition, but this reference has no validated rule for identifying a unique modern fulfillment date. Gītā 4.7–8 describes restoration age after age, not a dated countdown.
eschatology.dateability: No independently validated modern calendar date is supplied by this selected reference.

calendarNotes: A civil Saka label does not calculate regional Hindu festival rules. Regional tithi, sunrise and tradition choices require separately sourced algorithms or published dates.
limitations: No yuga epoch or duration is converted to an apocalypse date here.
An astronomical recurrence cannot independently validate the religious narrative.
Śaiva, Śākta and other Hindu accounts are outside this selected scope.

traditions.label: Buddhist traditions · Metteyya in DN 26
traditions.scope: Selected Pāli discourse in Bhikkhu Sujato’s translation; not every Buddhist school.
traditions.summary: DN 26 places the future Buddha Metteyya in a narrative of changed human conduct, lifespans and renewed flourishing.

eschatology.summary: DN 26:23–26 narrates Metteyya’s arising in a specified cosmological setting. Its lifespan figures are not an elapsed-years counter anchored to the present Gregorian year.
eschatology.dateability: No independently validated modern calendar date is supplied by this selected reference.

calendarNotes: A Thai Buddhist civil-era label is not a complete Buddhist lunar observance calendar. Vesak and other observances need regional published or calculated conventions.
limitations: One discourse does not represent all Theravāda, Mahāyāna or Vajrayāna accounts.
No near-term Maitreya date or literal demographic forecast is inferred.

traditions.label: Sikh tradition · selected conduct boundary
traditions.scope: SGPC English Sikh Rehat Maryada, Article XVI; cosmology not comprehensively assessed.
traditions.summary: The inspected discipline passage grounds conduct in the Guru’s tenets and explicitly rejects auspicious-day and horoscopic beliefs.

eschatology.summary: This selected source is a conduct code, not an eschatological timetable. No Sikh end-time claim is inferred from it, and no festival is given an astrological good/bad value.
eschatology.dateability: No independently validated modern calendar date is supplied by this selected reference.

calendarNotes: Article XVI(d), p.36, rejects belief in auspicious times/days and stellar or horoscopic influence. A sourced Sikh observance date must remain separate from astrology-purpose scores.
limitations: This is not a claim that the whole Sikh tradition lacks cosmological teachings.
No Nanakshahi festival dates are inferred from this conduct passage.

traditions.label: Jain traditions · an uncreated universe and liberation
traditions.scope: Selected scholarly accounts by Nalini Balbir and Mark Owen Webb.
traditions.summary: The checked accounts describe an uncreated, enduring universe, recurring time cycles and liberation of souls.

eschatology.summary: These accounts do not describe a single created world ending at a modern calendar deadline. Cosmic cycles and individual liberation are not converted into a near-term universal apocalypse.
eschatology.dateability: No independently validated modern calendar date is supplied by this selected reference.

calendarNotes: No Jain festival schedule is derived from a generic civil-calendar label. Sect and regional observance rules need their own sources.
limitations: Śvetāmbara and Digambara terminology and numerical details can differ.
The underlying primary scriptures were not newly collated; these are named scholarly summaries.

traditions.label: Bahá’í Faith · interpreted signs and a distinct calendar
traditions.scope: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, Some Answered Questions 26, plus the official calendar introduction.
traditions.summary: The selected authoritative Bahá’í chapter interprets return and judgment imagery through inner meanings, separately from its calculable observance calendar.

eschatology.summary: Some Answered Questions 26:5–6 says the cited signs have inner meanings and should not be read literally. This does not produce a future physical catastrophe date or make the interpretation Christian consensus.
eschatology.dateability: No independently validated modern calendar date is supplied by this selected reference.

calendarNotes: The official calendar describes sunset-to-sunset days, equinox-linked Naw-Rúz and Twin Birthdays after the eighth new moon. Published dated rows are handled separately; this reference computes none.
limitations: The separately cited Kitáb-i-Íqán was not newly read here.
Historical astronomical illustrations in the chapter are not reused as modern measurements.

traditions.label: Zoroastrian traditions · final renovation
traditions.scope: Zamyād Yašt 19 in Darmesteter’s translation, cross-read with Almut Hintze’s Iranica discussion.
traditions.summary: The selected texts describe frašō.kərəti, renovation of creation, resurrection and the overcoming of evil.

eschatology.summary: Yašt 19:89–96 and the selected Iranica discussion concern restoration and the savior tradition. They provide no independently validated Gregorian date for an event within this horizon.
eschatology.dateability: No independently validated modern calendar date is supplied by this selected reference.

calendarNotes: This eschatology reference does not choose among Fasli, Shahanshahi or Qadimi observance methods; a separately named source is needed for each date rule.
limitations: Textual layers and translations differ; a historical translation is not a complete account of present community belief.
No ancient cosmic chronology is silently converted into a modern deadline.

traditions.label: Shinto · hidden realm and local ritual continuity
traditions.scope: Kokugakuin’s Kakuriyo entry and Jinja Honcho’s Matsuri introduction; no survey of new religious movements.
traditions.summary: The selected sources discuss the hidden realm, kami and varied community rites rather than furnishing a universal end-of-world timetable.

eschatology.summary: Kakuriyo is explained as a hidden realm, not necessarily only an after-death world. The Matsuri source describes community and seasonal rites. Neither selected passage supplies a dated apocalypse; this limited reading is not proof that every Shinto-related movement lacks eschatology.
eschatology.dateability: No independently validated modern calendar date is supplied by this selected reference.

calendarNotes: Jinja Honcho explicitly notes substantial local variation between shrines. A universal Shinto festival schedule cannot be inferred from this introductory page.
limitations: Sect Shinto and Shinto-based new religions require separately named research.
Afterlife vocabulary, seasonal renewal and a world-ending prediction are different claim types.

traditions.label: Other selected tradition · historical Daoist Great Peace

traditions.summary: The selected scholarly discussion describes Great Peace ideals and historically situated messianic expectations in early Daoist movements.

eschatology.summary: The Taiping jing and early Laozi/Laojun expectations are described as historical traditions. They are not imported as a current Daoist prediction or as a future date for every Chinese community.
eschatology.dateability: No independently validated modern calendar date is supplied by this selected reference.

calendarNotes: Chinese civil lunar dates and publicly sourced festivals are separate from this historical doctrinal reference. Runtime conversion disagreements must not be resolved by eschatological claims.
limitations: The primary Taiping jing was not newly read; this is a selected scholarly account.
Confucian, folk-religious, Indigenous and other traditions are not comprehensively covered.
